It shouldn’t be this easy to pedal 25 mph: Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill?
  • These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark.
  • But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill? Should I switch to eco mode to preserve power and make sure I have enough to get home with the bike lights on?”.

These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark.

But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo. I didn’t experience range anxiety, even while blowing through city streets at 25-plus mph (40.2 kph). The bike has so much juice (840 watt-hours) and power (810 watts of peak power and 105 newton-meters of torque) from Specialized’s 3.1 motor system that I could ride as far and as fast as I wanted without worrying about having enough battery to get back home.

Recent findings suggest that given my preference for biking over driving, I need a bike that can get me across town at a decent clip without draining an entire charge. That’s exactly what the Evo delivered on my longest rides.

Recent findings suggest that what sold me on the bike was a 24-mile round trip that took 83 minutes and used just 56 percent of the battery. According to Specialized’s app, which connects to the bike over Bluetooth, I averaged 235 W of assist power while moving an average of 17 mph, though I was generally closer to 20 mph on stretches where I didn’t have to slow down. I also hit a max speed of 27.3 mph with little effort.

The bike is a beast, weighing around 70 pounds for the large-size frame I tested. Despite being the heaviest e-bike I’ve ridden, the Evo makes pedaling easier than ever. The bike lacks a throttle, so it takes a few rotations to get moving, but once the assist kicks in, it’s remarkable how easily you can reach the 18–20 mph range.

Recent findings suggest that that higher speed comes from the bike’s Sport mode, which became my default setting. It requires a bit more pedaling to reach full assist, which explains why my smartwatch recorded my heart rate in the moderate-to-vigorous zone if I was riding above 20 mph.) The other modes are Eco (minimal assist, with you supplying most of the power), Turbo (max power with little effort, making uphill climbs trivial), and Auto (which adjusts assist level to your pedaling). You can also tune each setting to your liking.

The added bulk is also meant to handle rougher terrain. I’ve had the occasional flat tire from road debris on slimmer bikes, so I appreciate the sturdier, all-terrain, flat-resistant tires. Still, the 70-pound frame makes me hesitant to venture too far from pavement. I won’t be bombing down any mountain bike trails, but it’s helpful to have the option to jump off a curb or ride on dirt or gravel roads.

Sources indicate that the weight makes the bike markedly different from the previous Turbo Vado we reviewed; this isn’t a bike I’d want to ride without assistance. Even the Eco mode, which you’d have to use exclusively to get the bike’s purported 150-km (93-mile), five-hour range, felt a bit sluggish compared to the more powerful modes I preferred. Specialized also sells a 280-Whr range extender, but at $700, it feels like overkill.

It has been revealed that the RockShox Psylo suspension fork, with 120 mm of travel, also made this the smoothest-riding e-bike I’ve tested. Other e-bikes I’ve ridden have felt stiff over even small bumps in the road, but the Evo’s bounciness made hitting bumps feel like a nice change of pace. I used to be scared of going over a curb, and that’s no longer the case. The 40 mm dropper seatpost is another nice feature, giving riders a bit of travel and letting them lower the seat to make it easier to touch the ground when stopped or dismounting.

Credit: Specialized Credit: Specialized.

While other e-bikes I’ve owned initially offered good range, storing them in colder weather has been an matter for their longevity.

So I’m grateful that Specialized made the downtube battery removable. Being able to store the battery in my house helps since I keep my bikes in an outdoor shed—I no longer have to worry about it sitting in freezing temperatures. A full charge takes four hours, though you can tweak the battery to cap charging at 80 percent to further extend its life.

Recent findings suggest that the other electric components are nice, too. On the Evo 5.0 I rode, a touchscreen lets you cycle through ride data, including your speed, estimated range remaining, and power assistance level. The front light even comes with low-beam (450 lumens) and high-beam (805 lumens) settings, making my night rides more visible.

In a recent development, if I have any complaints about my time with this bike, they boil down to two things. First, it’s incredibly heavy, making it difficult for many people to take up stairs. Second, the convenience of riding at high speed and making quick journeys has left my road bike gathering dust unless I’m specifically going out for a workout (and those are harder now that I’m so accustomed to riding the Evo). That’s more of a personal issue than a mark against the bike, though. It’s fun to ride, but maybe at the cost of consistent manual pedaling.

In a recent development, and then there’s the cost. I tested the Evo 5.0 ($5,200), which sits between the 4.0 ($4,500) and 6.0 ($7,000) in terms of cost, performance, and features. At $5,200, though, I would’ve liked to see a phone mount on the 5.0, which is a common enough feature on less-expensive bikes.

Recent findings suggest that those prices make securing the bike even more vital, and Specialized offers a few safety features to thwart theft. As mentioned, you can remove the battery, lock the back wheel, and disable the power system; there’s also Apple Find My integration if the bike ever escapes your purview (a bummer if you use Android, though).

It has been revealed that in all, Specialized has upgraded the e-bike experience enough for me to want to upgrade, though the price makes me blanch a bit. Maybe I can subsidize a purchase by selling an older e-bike.

Sony’s updated turntable is an easy entry into the world of vinyl

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Record players and other retro tech are making a strong comeback, and I’ve recently rejoined the world of vinyl collecting.
  • In a recent development, choosing a turntable can be quite overwhelming, especially for beginners.
  • Since 2019, Sony’s PS-LX310BT has been a go-to choice for vinyl newbies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Record players and other retro tech are making a strong comeback, and I’ve recently rejoined the world of vinyl collecting. Lately, I’ve noticed myself turning to Spotify less frequently, so it felt like the perfect time to start using a record player again.

In a recent development, choosing a turntable can be quite overwhelming, especially for beginners. That’s where Sony’s fresh PS-LX3BT turntable comes in.

Since 2019, Sony’s PS-LX310BT has been a go-to choice for vinyl newbies. Now that it has been discontinued, the PS-LX3BT emerges as its successor, keeping the same beginner-friendly approach while adding a few modern upgrades.

In a recent development, at the moment priced at $399.99, the PS-LX3BT is designed for people who want to enjoy vinyl without getting too caught up in the technical side of things. It’s also a good option for those looking to upgrade from their first inexpensive turntable without having to learn how to set up or customize a more complicated audio system.

One of its biggest selling points is how easy it is to use. The PS-LX3BT features automatic playback, so you simply press start and the tonearm lifts, moves into position, and drops onto the first track for you. There’s no need to manually position the needle or worry about getting everything just right. It’s a small convenience, but one that makes the experience much less intimidating for newcomers.

Sony has also made a few welcome changes compared with its predecessor. The PS-LX3BT now uses USB-C for power and supports Qualcomm’s aptX Adaptive Bluetooth codec, allowing it to transmit audio at up to 24-bit/96kHz. It also has a traditional phono output alongside Bluetooth, so you can choose between a wired speaker setup and listening wirelessly.

According to recent reports, one slightly strange design decision, however, is the repositioning of the start, stop, and tonearm buttons. On the older model, these were placed outside the dust cover. Now they’re underneath it, meaning you’ll have to lift the cover just to press start. It’s not a huge inconvenience, but still kind of annoying.

The turntable also offers USB connectivity for digitizing your vinyl collection. Connect it to a computer, and you can convert your records into digital audio files, which is useful if you want to preserve older records or listen to your collection on the go.

My biggest disappointment is the lack of a built-in speaker. It would have been nice to have everything included for someone just getting started. You’ll need to buy speakers (and possibly an amplifier) or compatible Bluetooth headphones separately, so keep that added cost in mind.

Industry observers note that if you’re searching for a more affordable and beginner-friendly automatic record player, there are cheaper options, such as this $179 option from Audio-Technica. But overall, Sony’s PS-LX3BT is a solid choice for anyone ready to dive into the world of vinyl for the first time.

Sources indicate that speaking of audio, the Sony WH-1000 XM5 headphones pack a versatile listening experience, bringing out the very best of lossless and hi-res music streaming. Its Active Noise Cancellation succeeds at drowning out pretty much everything around you, making them perfect for noisy commutes. At the same time, the Ambient Sound setting is useful for letting in outside noise while you listen to music, which you can easily enable and disable via the button on the left ear pad.

If there's anything to note, it would be the lack of collapsible ear pads, which are a fan-favorite feature from models past (it just makes it a lot easier for travelling). The Platinum Silver version is also prone to discoloring, so Black is probably the better shade to opt for, but other than that, they've presented zero disappointments.

#1580. The US Lost Its Measles Elimination Status. It’ll Take Years to Get It Back

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1128 w)

The US Lost Its Measles Elimination Status. It’ll Take Years to Get It Back

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: Two more people died from measles, bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and the country officially lost its status as a country that had eliminated the highly infectious disease.
  • The US eliminated measles in 2000 and maintained that status for 26 years.
  • Noel Brewer, a professor of health behavior at the University of North Carolina, presented a report last week to the Pan American Health Organization showing continuous measles transmission for at least 12 months in the US—erasing one of the nation’s greatest public health achievements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US has hit terrible twin milestones over the past week: Two more people died from measles, bringing this year’s death count to double digits, and the country officially lost its status as a country that had eliminated the highly infectious disease.

The US eliminated measles in 2000 and maintained that status for 26 years. Now, the nation faces an uphill battle to vanquish the virus once more, and it will take years to be measles-free again.

Noel Brewer, a professor of health behavior at the University of North Carolina, presented a report last week to the Pan American Health Organization showing continuous measles transmission for at least 12 months in the US—erasing one of the nation’s greatest public health achievements.

It has been revealed that WIRED asked him how he felt after PAHO officials reached a consensus that the country was no longer measles-free. He paused.

“I have not actually thought about my reaction,” he notes. After a beat, he says that the loss is “a somber moment for public health” that’s particularly wrenching because it’s a “completely avoidable situation.” Mexico and Canada have managed to wind down their outbreaks, but “measles in America is a runaway train,” Brewer says. “There's no end in sight, and it may even be gaining speed.”.

PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr. officially declared the change in status on Tuesday. “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” he said at a press conference. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.” Bolivia and Mexico also lost their elimination status this year; Canada lost it a year ago.

Recent findings suggest that brewer presented three key lines of evidence showing that measles has become endemic in the US. The outbreak in Utah and Arizona has gone on for more than 12 months, and the US has had measles cases every week since January 20, 2025. The genomic data also indicates a great deal of similarity across states, indicating the clusters are closely linked—and each week, there are cases where the sources can’t be confirmed, indicating they didn’t come from travel or known contact with other patients.

It has been revealed that “We have a problem on our hands,” states William Moss, epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins. And it’s not going away anytime soon. To reclaim its status as measles-free, the US will have to prove it has gone a full year without continued transmission. That’s unlikely to happen under the Trump administration—and its actions have made it more difficult for future leaders.

“Reestablishing elimination is not just about reporting fewer cases—it also requires convincing the world that we have a strong enough surveillance system to find cases and deaths,” Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University, tells WIRED in a text.

In a recent development, the fact that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments differ on how many people have died from measles “is a sign of dysfunction,” Nuzzo says. There have been 10 confirmed measles deaths so far this year—seven in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, and one in New York—but the CDC only lists six.

Such chaos also breeds distrust, indicates Frederic Bertley, president and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry. That's “a huge problem” for a public trying to parse who is telling the truth and whether they should listen, he says.

Even as measles was eliminated, anti-vaccine rhetoric began to rise, especially around the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Vaccination rates began falling—spurred in part by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an environmental lawyer turned anti-vaccine activist who published a now-retracted article alleging a link between vaccines and autism in 2005. He continued crusading against vaccines as head of Children’s Health Defense and at the helm of the Department of Health and Human Services during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration has done little to stop the outbreaks, cutting billions in funding from state, local, territorial, and tribal public health departments and offering conflicting messages on vaccines. During a televised February 2025 cabinet meeting following the first child death in a decade, Kennedy mentioned “it's not unusual, we have measles outbreaks every year.” The CDC hasn’t held a single press conference on measles throughout the entire outbreak; as PAHO was making its measles status announcement on Tuesday, HHS sent out an email about Kennedy’s cooking show.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz stated in a statement. “Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Kennedy posted on X, “I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”.

To regain its elimination status, the US needs to address barriers to health care access, missed vaccination opportunities, misinformation, and vaccine hesitancy, Barbosa mentioned. That includes mounting wide-reaching vaccination campaigns, expanding laboratory testing capacity, and responding swiftly to cases, including contact tracing. It’s the bread and butter of public health, but the longer it takes to create a comprehensive response, the more it will cost, experts warn.

According to recent reports, future efforts to contain measles will require “a stronger centralized federal response to these outbreaks” paired with support for “very local responses,” notes Moss. That means identifying communities with long-standing under-vaccination and understanding why, he says, as well as improving trust in public health guidance.

“Immunity gaps” tend to concentrate in specific geographic areas and communities, and national or even state-level data can “mask these significant inequalities, providing an incomplete picture of the population's actual level of protection,” Barbosa mentioned.

The CDC announced $100 million in August and September—more than a year after the outbreak began—to help fund state and regional efforts to combat measles, but Congress will need to allocate $100 million to $400 million more for measles elimination in coming months, Brewer says.

Recent findings suggest that “More than 90 percent of children get the measles vaccine, Brewer points out. “This is a vaccine that has extraordinary public support, and it goes across the aisle.”.

But to achieve herd immunity, vaccination rates need to be at least 95 percent due to how contagious the disease is. High transmissibility also means measles is very hard to uproot once it begins to spread.

According to recent reports, yet ending national measles transmission is “its own reward,” Brewer claims. It spares children’s lives, keeps them out of hospitals, and prevents blindness and other lifelong complications. “We no longer have that benefit,” he says. “Children are now being stalked by this incurable and deadly disease.”.

It cites research showing most large companies give AI security to someone who already has another job.

Vero Security, a year-old startup that helps companies control the AI tools and agents their staff use, has raised an $11M seed round, it announced on Wednesday. TLV Partners led the round, with GTM Capital, Maple Capital and angel investors joining. Vero, based in Latest York and Tel Aviv, claims several Fortune 500 companies already use it.

Industry observers note that its main product checks prompts and actions as AI agents run, and blocks those that break tech giant rules. For example, it can stop a coding agent reading keys it has no need for, the kind of leaked tokens behind last month’s LiteLLM hack. Security teams set the policy, and Vero turns it into controls that upgrade as AI tools change.

“CISOs have seen enough dashboards and tables that tell their teams what’s wrong and leave the work to them,” said co-founder and CEO Elad Tessler.

Tessler previously led product at Astrix Security, which Cisco bought this year. Vero is also launching a free online course and community for AI security staff, which it states contains no sales material.

In a recent development, the field is crowded. Zenity raised $125M in August, Tel Aviv’s Bay raised $50M last week, and Pluto Security emerged with $42M in October. Security teams often cannot see the AI their companies use.

#1575. Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA.
  • MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning.
  • Industry observers note that “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright notes by way of example in the release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories.

MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.

Industry observers note that “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright notes by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?”.

In an accompanying announcement video, Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.”.

Wright said MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.

According to recent reports, since this is 2026, it shouldn’t be surprising that MyMems is making heavy use of generative AI (with a “proprietary behavior engine” on top) to transform your typed-up memories into simulated locales and characters. In the announcement video, Wright praises the “entirely open-ended” AI systems Gallium is using “to extract from the stories and whatnot based upon the memories you put into the game.”.

But Wright’s focus on mining memories for simulation content predates the current generative AI boom. What has now become MyMems started off as Proxi, a mobile simulation that was first declared in 2018 as “a game of self-discovery, a game where we actually uncover the hidden you.” But after years of pre-production work (as outlined in an excellent Vulture piece earlier this year), Wright’s Gallium Studios finally ran out of funding in late 2024, leading to mass layoffs for the small team and an uncertain future for the project.

Recent findings suggest that now the idea has been revived thanks in large part to a partnership with AI middleware firm Artificial Agency. Until now, that tech giant has mainly been focused on agentic systems that can create “virtual players” to playtest a game or serve as a partner for human players.

Now, Artificial Agency’s marketing says the tech giant’s AI tool will be used to create “a personal behavior model and a knowledge graph” from players’ memories, drawing some unsettling comparisons to big tech surveillance.

“Meta knows what you click,” the organization writes. “Netflix knows what you watch. Nobody knows what you remember. MemDNA learns from your memories locally and only with your permission.”.

Wright remarked the partnership with Artificial Agency will let Gallium benefit from “off-the-shelf” AI solutions without having to “become an AI research company” in its own right. He also said the collaboration will help limit costs by providing a cheaper option than the “really expensive” frontier models that might be overkill for a project like this.

“Right now AI has opened a vast new design area and I’m enjoying, you know, exploring that as a designer,” Wright mentioned.
